_comment: Build-time feature gates. Edit and rebuild to change. allow_delete_user exposes the destructive 'delete_user.sh' entry in the Scripts menu; keep it false unless the build is intended for admins who need it. primary_bastion_filter / secondary_bastion_filter narrow the bastion dropdowns in every Scripts dialog (create_new_user, delete_user, and Vault IAM Access) to instances whose name or id contains the given text (case-insensitive); empty shows all. protected_users are never deleted by delete_user (case-insensitive); the script also hardcodes system-account protection as a backstop.
_vault_iam_comment: "Vault IAM Access" entry in the Scripts menu. It opens a dialog (IAM role ARN, policy HCL, AWS role name, policy name, environment, primary/secondary bastion, VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TOKEN), then on the PRIMARY bastion writes the policy, writes auth/aws/role/<name> bound to the IAM role, and reads both back to verify. It reuses primary_bastion_filter / secondary_bastion_filter above for the bastion dropdowns. allowed_users lists the OS usernames that see the entry: ["*"] = everyone (the shipped default), [] = nobody, or name specific users to restrict it. The Environment dropdown lists ACCOUNT -> ENVIRONMENT pairs (an account can host more than one environment, told apart by each instance's MMODAL_ENV tag), and picking one narrows both bastion dropdowns to that environment's instances. VAULT_ADDR is pre-filled from the selected environment's "vault_addr" in accounts.json, falling back to the account-level "vault_addr", and is editable; environments with neither open with a blank box that must be filled in by hand. The VAULT_TOKEN is typed per run and is NEVER stored — not in this file, not in config.ini.
_vault_iam_delete_comment: "Vault IAM Delete" is the flip of Vault IAM Access: same dialog minus the ARN and policy boxes, it runs 'vault delete auth/aws/role/<name>' + 'vault policy delete <name>' on the primary bastion, lists the remaining roles, and confirms both objects are gone. Meant for tearing down a test role before re-running the create. It is DESTRUCTIVE, so it has its own list and ships empty (nobody). A user must be on BOTH allowed_users and delete_allowed_users to see it — being able to create does not imply being able to delete. Add usernames to delete_allowed_users and rebuild to hand it out.
_user_sync_comment: "Bastion User Sync" entry in the Scripts menu. Both bastions mount the same EFS at /efs/home, and NFS authorises by NUMBER rather than by name, so an account is only usable on both boxes when its uid AND gid are identical on both. Drift arrives when someone creates an account on one bastion and not the other: that box then hands the next new user a number the other box has already spent, and the create fails on the secondary with 'UID nnnn is not unique', leaving a half-made account. NOTE that Bastion New User already does this check automatically -- every create reads both bastions first, creates anything missing from either, and allocates a uid/gid free on both -- so this dialog is for auditing, and for repairing drift without creating anyone. It scans a chosen environment's primary and secondary, reports every account with a home under /efs/home, and creates the ones missing from either side using the SAME uid/gid, but only where both numbers are free on the target. It never renumbers an account whose uid differs between the boxes (that needs usermod plus a recursive chown of a live home on a shared filesystem) and never takes over a number held by someone else (that needs useradd --non-unique, which makes two people one identity on EFS); both are reported for a human to settle. allowed_users lists the OS usernames that see the entry: ["*"] = everyone, [] = nobody (the shipped default), or name specific users. It writes accounts on both bastions, so it ships closed -- add usernames and rebuild to hand it out..
_alerts_comment: On-call Alerts button (Jira Service Management Operations). cloud_id + email identify the JSM site to query. allowed_users lists the OS usernames (Windows USERNAME / Linux USER, matched case-insensitively) that may see the Alerts button; use ["*"] for everyone, [] to hide it from everyone. The button only appears when cloud_id AND email are set AND the user is on the list. DO NOT commit a real API token in 'token' — this file is in git. Leave it empty and have each user set JIRA_TOKEN in their environment; JIRA_TOKEN always overrides this value.
_personal_scripts_comment: "Add Script" in the Scripts menu (save your own shell scripts, optionally bound to a hotkey, that paste into the focused connection tab) is available to everyone. This section instead gates the git integration: users on allowed_users are prompted once for a git personal access token, get git's credential store on the remote box populated by Prep Terminal (scoped to git_host, so git clone/pull over HTTPS just work), and receive the hardcoded default_scripts below (e.g. a Ctrl+1 're-clone the repo' script). Users NOT on the list can still create their own scripts and bind Ctrl+1 themselves. Matching: OS username, case-insensitive, ["*"] = everyone, [] = nobody (the shipped default). The PAT is cached in the user's local config.ini (base64, not encrypted) — never in this file. default_scripts fields: name, hotkey (e.g. "Ctrl+1"), body (the shell script; the credential store makes the clone auth automatically). In a body, {{user}} is replaced with the local OS username (the allowed_users name) before it runs — use it for per-user paths like /home/efs/{{user}}, since the remote $USER is the SSM/root account, not the person running the app.
_access_email_comment: Post-create Outlook access email (Windows only). Discover the encrypt_* values with scripts/outlook_verification.ps1 (or test_headless_encrypt.ps1), then paste them here. Headless encryption needs all three: encrypt_permission (the MailItem.Permission value it reported, e.g. 3), encrypt_permission_service (1 = olWindows), and encrypt_template_guid (the tenant RMS/IRM template GUID, same for everyone in your org - keep the braces). encrypt_smime_flag is only used when there is no template GUID (1 = S/MIME encrypt). encrypt_sendkeys is the QAT Encrypt shortcut for the visible fallback path (Alt+6 = '%6'). Set enabled=false to turn the feature off. auto_run makes the app run the script itself as soon as a create finishes with a saved PEM; set it to false to leave the 'Send Email Command' menu as the only route. email_domains lists your organization's MAIL domains (e.g. ["xyz.com","old-xyz.com"]): a recipient that resolves outside all of them is never mailed unattended, which stops a stale local Contacts entry or autocomplete cache hit from receiving the PEM. Staff often have mail on more than one domain, and this is unrelated to the Windows/AD domain the machine is joined to. A single string or a comma-separated string also works. Leave it empty to skip that check. email_local_format checks the SHAPE of the resolved address against the username, catching an in-domain address that belongs to a different person with a similar name (the domain check cannot): 'flast' means first initial + surname with an optional number, so john.smith accepts jsmith@ or jsmith2@ but not johnsmith@. Leave it empty to skip.
_fed_auth_comment: Automatic 'fed up' credential refresh. Triggered by EXPIRY, not a timer: the app watches fed_expire in ~/.aws/credentials and runs fed up when it lapses, so backdating that value is a realistic way to test. A failure retries every retry_interval_secs for up to retry_window_secs, then stands down and waits for you to sign in by hand; it arms itself again as soon as the credentials file is renewed. allowed_users matches the HOST account the GUI runs as (%USERNAME% on Windows, $USER on Linux) -- NOT the login inside an embedded WSL or SSM terminal, and not your AWS or Okta username. The app logs the name it detected and every gate's verdict at startup ('gates: os_user=...'), so check the log panel if a feature does not appear. 'command' is argv, so ["fed","up"] runs `fed up` -- on Windows it goes through `cmd /C` so the name resolves via PATHEXT exactly as it does at a prompt, which is what makes a fed.bat or fed.cmd wrapper work. auto_sign_in drives the Okta page itself (types the code, the username, and the password from Windows Credential Manager, then confirms MFA) instead of handing you the activation page. It has its own allow-list, auto_sign_in_allowed_users, so a site can give everyone the refresh and only named users the automation -- a user needs 'enabled', a place on allowed_users, 'auto_sign_in', AND a place on auto_sign_in_allowed_users. IT IS OFF BY DEFAULT WITH AN EMPTY LIST ON PURPOSE: typing a domain password into an identity provider and clicking through MFA is behaviour an EDR scores as credential theft, and this app has a CrowdStrike quarantine in its history. With it off the feature still runs fed up on expiry, opens the page and copies the code, and never synthesises a keystroke. With it on it is the primary path but falls back to open-and-copy if the script is missing, the vault is empty, or the focus guard trips. The password lives ONLY in Windows Credential Manager: the app cannot write, test for or delete it and never sees the plaintext, so you set it yourself with cmdkey /generic:ec2-manager-fed /user:<your-okta-user> /pass, or Control Panel -> Credential Manager -> Windows Credentials -> 'Add a generic credential'. It must be GENERIC, not a 'Windows credential'. The /user: value recorded with it is what gets typed on the Okta username page. chrome_args goes to Chrome ahead of the URL. --new-window is the default and matters: with Chrome already running a bare 'chrome.exe <url>' opens a TAB in whatever window exists -- possibly minimised, behind others, or on another virtual desktop -- and the sign-in then times out waiting for a foreground page that loaded fine but nowhere it could be typed into. A separate profile (--user-data-dir) is deliberately NOT the default, because remembered-device cookies live in the profile and a fresh one invites more verification, not less. close_browser_on_success shuts the window the sign-in drove once fed up reports the credentials renewed; it closes that WINDOW (WM_CLOSE to its handle), never the chrome.exe process, which with --new-window is usually shared with the rest of your browsing. It only ever closes a window the automation itself opened and drove. mfa_process_match widens the guard for the FINAL step only: Okta Verify owns the confirm prompt in its own borderless centred window, which looks like a Chrome popup but is a separate process, so a chrome-only guard stops one keystroke from done. That step types no secret (a bare Enter); every step that types the code, username or password still requires Chrome. browser_title_match is the focus guard: nothing is typed unless the foreground window is Chrome AND its title contains one of these fragments. It is a LIST because the sign-in walks several pages (activation, username, password, MFA) that do not share a title -- a single fragment matching the first page will abort on a later one. The guard waits up to 10s for a match rather than sampling one instant, so page transitions are not a race. If a step aborts, the error names the actual window title; add a fragment of it here. run_timeout_secs bounds a single fed up: it blocks until the device authorization is approved, so a sign-in nobody completes would pin the worker and, since only one run happens at a time, block every later expiry until the app restarts. access_retry_interval_secs covers a different failure: the sign-in worked, but fed reports no access to one account and prints a URL to request it. That is an entitlement usually landing within a minute, so it retries every 30s rather than the general 120s -- detection requires BOTH the wording and a URL, so an ordinary 'not authorized' that will never resolve is not retried hard for the whole window. Zero timings mean use the defaults (120 / 600 / 300 / 30 seconds).
